To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
voltage-dependent modulation of IP(3) receptors is an important factor that can synchronize Ca(2+) waves across cells that are electrically coupled through gap junctions.

electrical coupling acting via voltage-dependent modulation of Ca(2+), and not diffusion of Ca(3+) or the second messengers IP(3), can synchronize oscillations of Ca(2+)/IP(3) across large distances in a tissue.

electrical coupling acting though voltage-dependent modulation of IP(3) receptors is able to synchronize Ca(2+) waves across cells even when the cells are widely separated, and have different intrinsic oscillation frequencies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that synchronize oscillations of intracellular Ca(II) concentration in the smooth muscle cells of the gastrointestinal tract.
the role of electrical coupling in synchronization of intracellular Ca( 2+) oscillations and the generation of rhythmic depolarization of smooth muscle cells.
the role of electrical coupling in synchronization of Ca oscillations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
voltage-dependent modulation of Ca(2+), acting through the IP(3) receptors, is able to entrain store Ca(2+).
voltage-dependent modulation of IP(3)-sensitive Ca(2+) channels is a novel mechanism that may play an important role in the synchronization of Ca( 2+) oscillations in smooth muscle cells.
the voltage-dependent modulation of IP(3)-induced Ca2+ release is a significant mechanism for synchronization of Ca2+, and hence membrane, oscillations in smooth muscle cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electrical coupling acting through modulation of store Ca²⁺ release is able to entrain Ca²⁺ oscillations in smooth muscle cells.
the voltage-dependent enhancement of Ca(2+), and thus the Ca(2+)-(IP3)-Ca(2+) feedback mechanism, can be an important component in the synchronization of Ca(²+) oscillations in smooth muscle.

electrical coupling acting on voltage-dependent modulation of Ca(2+)(i) store oscillations can synchronize oscillations across large distances and can synchronize oscillations in cells with different intrinsic frequencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
voltage-dependent modulation of Ca(2+), acting through IP(3) receptors, is a mechanism that is able to synchronize store Ca(2+).
voltage dependence of store Ca( 2+ ) release can synchronize oscillations of distant cells even in the absence of chemical coupling.
electrical coupling acting on IP(3) receptors is a mechanism that is able to synchronize store Ca(2+), and thus slow-wave, oscillations in a wide variety of cells.
